claims.text: Tungsten is the plasma-facing material and CuCrZr is the lower-temperature heat sink.
A tungsten-based HEA is used as the intermediate layer between plasma-facing tungsten and CuCrZr.
The intervention is to introduce 5–10 vol.% well-dispersed Cu nanoparticles into the tungsten-based HEA during synthesis.
Cu nanoparticle incorporation will improve heat transfer without compromising structural integrity under plasma-facing reactor conditions.
The relevant service conditions are approximately 350–600 °C with cyclic high heat flux and moderate irradiation.
Uniformly distributed Cu nanoparticles will act as localized, highly conductive pathways in the HEA.
The Cu nanoparticles will remain coherently bonded to the HEA matrix and mediate load transfer.
Copper has high intrinsic thermal conductivity.
Cu nanoparticles create additional electron- and phonon-transport channels in the tungsten-based HEA.
Copper's ductility will maintain toughness and suppress crack propagation in the composite.
The Cu-doped layer will have approximately 20–30% greater effective thermal conductivity than the undoped tungsten-based HEA.
The Cu-doped layer will retain mechanical strength comparable to the undoped HEA.
The Cu-doped layer will retain resistance to irradiation-induced degradation comparable to the undoped HEA.
Current monolithic tungsten-based HEA intermediate layers have suboptimal heat transfer.
Monolithic tungsten-based HEAs have excellent radiation resistance and thermomechanical stability.
The beneficial effects will persist from 350 to 600 °C under cyclic heat flux.
Excessive Cu segregation at higher temperature or during prolonged irradiation could compromise performance.
Nanoparticle agglomeration or phase separation may occur over extended service times.
A controlled comparison will use Cu-doped and undoped layers made by identical processing routes and exposed to the same thermal, heat-flux, and irradiation conditions.
Failure to achieve a statistically significant thermal-conductivity improvement of at least about 10%, or significant degradation of tensile strength or creep resistance, will falsify the hypothesis.
